newsitem.title: USA: Looking for the perfect stock fund.
newsitem.headline: Looking for the perfect stock fund.

text.p: It should be easy to find at least a few mutual funds that are perfect. After all, there are some 6,544 stock funds available to investors, according to Morningstar Inc.
The hardest part is deciding just what makes a perfect stock fund. Here are a few criteria that seasoned fund pickers suggest:

-- At least five years of above-average gains. Only 1,376 of the 6,544 stock funds out there have been around for five years or longer. And just 666 of them have above-average gains during the period.

Why five years? Because that's barely long enough for a fund to show its stuff in different market environments. For example, a fund that does well in a market that favours blue-chip growth stocks might go completely to pieces when the small-cap sector returns to favour.

-- A manager who has been around for at least five years. What good is a strong record if the manager who built it has moved on? Only 308 of the 666 stock funds pass this hurdle, which is no surprise.
Many top managers jump ship to start their own funds. At Fidelity and other big companies, the brightest young fund managers often get promoted to bigger funds on a regular basis.

-- It's small. Here's where we run into real problems. Small funds have an enormous advantage over bigger ones: Their managers can invest all of the funds' assets in their favourite stocks. By contrast, there is no way for a $5 billion fund to buy only stocks that its manager loves. The fund has to spread those assets among hundreds of companies' shares--and there is no way for any manager or team to really keep tabs on that many companies.

Trouble is, any fund that has delivered superior returns over the past five years is likely to be big, unless it has closed to new investors, in which case you can't get in. In fact, there are only 168 five-year-old funds with less than $500 million in assets.

-- Less volatility than its typical peer. If you are a truly long-term investor, you may not care about this one. It doesn't in theory matter if your fund's share price fluctuates in the short term, as long as you get the long-term returns you need to meet your goals. But in practice, wouldn't you prefer a fund that offers a relatively smooth ride?

Some experts argue that you must accept higher risk to get higher returns, but that simply isn't true. In fact, there are funds that consistently post above-average returns while taking below-average risk. Their managers do it by making long-term investments in undervalued stocks.

-- Low expenses. Expenses may seem like no big deal when the market soars 20 percent or 30 percent in a single year. But taken over time, a high expense ratio can chip away at your returns. The average stock fund has annual expenses equal to around 1.67 percent of assets; thus, you should shoot for something lower than that.

-- An intelligent strategy that you understand. A fund can get lucky and stay lucky for years. Thus, you should choose one that invests according to a method that makes sense to you -- one that you are convinced will continue to work over the long run.

Many funds have generated big gains in recent years by investing in the hottest stocks their managers could find. Such momentum investing has made several fund managers into stars, and drawn billions of dollars into their funds. But how intelligent is it to buy the hottest stock of the day without considering whether you are paying too much for it? Fact is, that approach is bound to backfire sooner or later. When it does, you don't want to be holding the bag.

Funds that you can rely upon to deliver solid long-term returns typically are run by managers who give some thought to the concept of value. What is a stock really worth? What kinds of earnings can the company deliver over time? How strong are the company's products, markets, management and balance sheet? Such questions aren't often asked these days; instead, managers want to know how far a stock has climbed and how fast.

In the end, only 41 funds meet all of the above criteria. Among those funds are offerings such as Homestead Value (800-258-3030; $1,000 minimum investment; no load). Value-oriented manager Stuart Teach has run the fund since its inception in 1990. During the past five years, he's provided shareholders with 40 percent higher gains than the typical equity fund, with about 30 percent less volatility. What's more, the fund's assets are only $325 million, and its expense ratio is a low 0.73 percent.

Another solid choice is Vontobel U.S. Value (800-527-9500; $1,000 minimum; no load), with assets of only $103 million. It has gained 17.1 percent annually during the past five years, vs. 14.5 percent for its typical competitor. Manager Ed Walczak insists on sound companies with strong franchises and predictable earnings whose shares are selling at reasonable levels.
(Clint Willis is a free-lance writer who covers mutual funds for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Willis.)
